610.title: Upasiva's question
610.hook: one of the sixteen asks what to rely on to cross; the Buddha answers, nothingness, mindfully
610.howItsDone: Teachers often cite Upasiva's question when explaining nibbana as the flame gone out, and the image of the flame that can no longer be reckoned is common in Theravada teaching on what can and cannot be said of the awakened.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Parayana, sixteen students walking north to ask their questions. Your line: crossing the flood. Today, one of the sixteen asks his.

Upasiva is the sixth of the sixteen to speak. His question is short, and plain. Alone, he says, with nothing to hold on to, I can't cross the great flood. Tell me something to lean on. It's a sentence that could be said at the edge of anything too big: a diagnosis, a debt, a loss. Not what is the meaning of life. Just: what do I hold?
screen: `THE SIXTH OF THE SIXTEEN.` → `ALONE, I CAN'T CROSS.` → `TELL ME SOMETHING TO LEAN ON.`

segments.voice: The Buddha's answer is surprising. Mindful, he says, looking to nothingness, leaning on the thought there is nothing, cross the flood. Let go of sense-desires, step back from talk, and watch, day and night, for the end of craving. Upasiva had meditated deeply; the commentary says he already knew the meditation called the base of nothingness. So the Buddha meets him there, in the place he already knows, and adds the one thing that turns it from a resting place into a crossing: mindfulness. Upasiva asks more. If someone stays there, would he become cool and freed right there, or would his consciousness pass on? The Buddha gives an image. As a flame blown out by the wind goes to rest and can't be counted any more, so the sage, freed, goes to rest and can't be counted. Does he not exist then, Upasiva asks, or is he forever well? There's no measuring the one who has gone to rest, the Buddha says. When everything is uprooted, every way of speaking about him is uprooted too. That last answer refuses both easy options. And with it, this path leaves the Sutta Nipata: from the snake shedding its skin, through the herdsman in the rain, the rhinoceros, the jewel, the blessings, the poet, the dart, the eights, all the way to this crossing. Tomorrow, a new book, of joy.

segments.voice: Notice what you usually lean on when things get hard: your phone, a plan, someone's reassurance; you don't have to give any of them up. For now, lean on nothing but knowing what's happening: breath in, known; breath out, known; a sound, known. When the mind reaches for a handhold, notice the reaching, and come back.

611.title: Inspired sayings
611.hook: short verses the Buddha spoke from joy, each with its story
611.howItsDone: The Udana is read and taught in Theravada communities, and its verses are sometimes chanted.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Upasiva's question, and the flame gone to rest. Your line: mindful, cross. The Sutta Nipata is done; today a new book opens.

Some things you say on purpose. Others just come out. You round a bend on a hike and the whole valley opens, and before you've decided anything you've said, oh. A friend tells you good news and you laugh out loud. Those words aren't planned. They're breathed out. The early Buddhist canon has a whole book built from moments like that: times when something happened, the Buddha saw what it meant, and a few lines of verse came out of him. The book takes its name from that breathing out.
screen: `SOME WORDS JUST COME OUT.` → `THE VALLEY OPENS: OH.` → `A BOOK OF THOSE MOMENTS.`

segments.voice: Tradition explains udana as a breathing out, and the word means a heartfelt utterance, words spoken from a full heart, often from joy. The book is part of the Khuddaka Nikaya, the collection of short books, alongside the Dhammapada and the Sutta Nipata you've just finished. It has eighty discourses, in eight chapters of ten, and every one follows the same shape, which makes it easy to read. First, a short story in prose: where the Buddha was, who came, what happened. Then a formula, repeated eighty times: knowing the meaning of this, the Buddha, on that occasion, spoke this inspired saying. Then the verse. The story is the soil and the verse is what grows from it. The stories are often small and human: a woman in a long, hard labor; a monk homesick for his bride; boys at a pond; moths at a lamp. A few hold teachings this path will spend whole days on, starting tomorrow. One more thing. Not every udana is joyful in the everyday sense. Some come from sorrow, some from seeing something hard. But in every one, the verse comes after the Buddha sees what the moment means.

612.title: Doubts vanish
612.hook: after awakening he reviews dependent origination, and doubts vanish like mist
612.tomorrow: In the seen, only the seen
612.howItsDone: Dependent origination is taught across Buddhist schools, and some Theravada chanting books set out its links in forward and reverse order, as in the opening of the Udana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Udana, a book of words breathed out from a full heart. Your line: spoken from joy. Today, its very first udana.

The book doesn't start with a crowd or a sermon. It starts under a tree. The Buddha has just awakened, at Uruvela, on the bank of the Neranjara river, at the foot of the bodhi tree. For seven days, the text says, he sits there in one cross-legged posture, feeling the happiness of release. No teaching yet. No students. Just a man sitting by a river for a week. At the end of those seven days, he does something very specific with his mind, through the watches of the night.
screen: `UNDER THE TREE, BY THE RIVER.` → `SEVEN DAYS IN ONE POSTURE.` → `THEN, THREE WATCHES OF THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: In the first watch of the night, he attends to dependent origination in forward order: when this is, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. Ignorance gives rise to formations, formations to consciousness, and so on, link by link, to the whole mass of suffering. And the verse comes: when things become clear to the one who meditates with ardor, his doubts all vanish, because he understands a thing together with its cause. The next udana: the same, in reverse. When this is not, that does not come to be; with the ending of this, that ends. Doubts vanish, because he understands the ending of causes. The third: both directions together. And this time the verse adds an image: he stands, scattering Mara's army, like the sun lighting up the sky. Notice how doubt goes in this story. Not by being argued with, or pushed down. It goes because something is seen: this comes from that. Elsewhere the early texts list doubt among the hindrances: the wobbling that can't decide. What ends it isn't certainty about everything. It's seeing one cause clearly. Mist doesn't need to be fought. The sun comes up, and it's gone.

segments.voice: Pick one feeling that's here right now, a bit of tiredness, worry, a flicker of irritation, and ask gently where it came from: a short night, a message you read? Follow it one link back, then one more if it's there, without analyzing too hard. Just see that this came from that, and notice whether the feeling changes when its cause is seen.
Doubts vanish. The first three udanas: when the Buddha sees how each thing arises from its cause, his doubts vanish, and in the third verse he shines like the sun lighting up the sky.
Your line: see one cause clearly. Fog thins when the light comes. Day six hundred twelve.

613.title: In the seen, only the seen
613.hook: to Bahiya: in the seen, only the seen; in the heard, only the heard
613.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in Theravada and other traditions often give the Bahiya instruction as a practice of bare attention: noting what is seen, heard, sensed and known, without adding to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: doubts vanish, three watches of the night under the tree. Your line: see one cause clearly. Today, a teaching only a few lines long, given on a city street.

On the coast at Supparaka lives a man called Bahiya of the bark cloth, because he dresses in strips of bark. People honor him and bring him food and robes; many think he's fully awakened. One day he wonders it himself. And a deity who wishes him well, the text says, tells him plainly: you're not, and you're not even on the way. But in Savatthi, far to the north, there's someone who is. Bahiya sets out at once; the text says he never stayed more than one night anywhere on the way. At the monastery he's told the Teacher has gone into town for alms. So he follows him into the street.
screen: `BAHIYA OF THE BARK CLOTH.` → `YOU'RE NOT EVEN ON THE WAY.` → `HE FOLLOWS HIM INTO THE STREET.`

segments.voice: Bahiya finds the Buddha walking for alms, falls at his feet, and asks: teach me. It's not the time, the Buddha says; we've come into town for alms. Bahiya asks again, and gives his reason: life is uncertain, yours and mine. Not the time, the Buddha says again. A third time Bahiya asks. And there in the street, alms bowl in hand, the Buddha gives him a teaching only a few lines long. Train yourself like this, Bahiya. In the seen, there will be only the seen. In the heard, only the heard. In the sensed, only the sensed. In the known, only the known. When that's so, you won't be with it. When you're not with it, you won't be in it. Then you'll be neither here nor beyond nor in between. That is the end of suffering. Look at the first line. You see a face in a crowd, and instantly the mind adds: she's frowning at me, I must have done something, I always do this. The seen was a face. Everything else was added. The teaching asks Bahiya to stop at the face: not to stop seeing, but to stop building on top of it. When nothing is added, there's no I standing in the middle, taking it personally. Then the Buddha walks on with his bowl.

segments.voice: Rest your open eyes on something near you, a cup, a patch of wall, and let it be only what's seen: color, shape, light. When the mind adds a name, a story or an opinion, notice that it's added and come back. Then close your eyes and do the same with sound, letting a passing car be just a rising and falling sound.
Dittha, the seen. The Buddha's teaching to Bahiya: in the seen, only the seen; in the heard, only the heard; nothing added, and no one in the middle.
Your line: stop at the face. The rest of the story can wait. More of Bahiya tomorrow.

614.title: No time to lose
614.hook: Bahiya awakens on the spot, and dies soon after, gored by a cow
614.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers sometimes tell Bahiya's story to illustrate appamada, heedfulness, and Theravada tradition, following the canon's list, remembers him as the disciple foremost in quick understanding.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dittha, the seen, and Bahiya taught in the street. Your line: stop at the face. Today, how his story ends.

Someday I'll call my aunt. Someday I'll start sitting every morning. Someday I'll say sorry for that thing in college. A someday list feels safe because it assumes there's time. Bahiya didn't assume it. When the Buddha told him twice that it wasn't the time, his answer was blunt: life is uncertain, yours and mine. He'd come a long way to hear the teaching, and he wasn't willing to wait until after lunch. Today, how the story ends, and why it ends so fast.
screen: `THE SOMEDAY LIST.` → `LIFE IS UNCERTAIN, YOURS AND MINE.` → `NOT AFTER LUNCH.`

segments.voice: The text says that as he heard those few lines, in the seen only the seen, Bahiya's mind was freed, right there in the street. Then the Buddha went on with his alms round. And not long after, a cow with a young calf attacked Bahiya and killed him. That's the whole of it, in one sentence. On his way back, the Buddha saw the body. He asked the monks to carry it on a litter, to cremate it, and to build a memorial mound for him. When the monks asked what had become of Bahiya, the Buddha said: he was wise; he practiced in line with the teaching; he didn't trouble me with questions about it. He has reached final release. Elsewhere in the canon, in a list of outstanding disciples, Bahiya is named foremost among those who understood quickly. Sit with the shape of the story. A man traveled far, asked three times, heard a few lines, understood them, and died soon after. If he had waited for the right time, there would have been no time. The early texts have a word for this kind of alertness: appamada, heedfulness, not letting things slide. It doesn't mean panic. Bahiya wasn't frantic; he was clear. It means the good thing you can do today is today's.

segments.voice: Let your someday list come to mind, and find one small item on it: a message, a thank you, an apology, a few minutes of sitting. Picture yourself doing it today, where and when. Then rest with the breath, calm, not hurried, knowing it's waiting for you.
Appamada, heedfulness. Bahiya asked to be taught at once, because life is uncertain; he understood at once, and died soon after.
Your line: today is today's. Being heedful doesn't mean being hurried. Day six hundred fourteen, done.

615.title: The boys and the fish
615.hook: boys tormenting fish; would you want pain?
615.howItsDone: The first of the five precepts lay Buddhists undertake is to refrain from killing living beings, and teachers sometimes explain it, as here, by putting oneself in the other's place.

segments.voice: Yesterday: appamada, heedfulness, and how Bahiya's story ended. Your line: today is today's. Today, a scene by the road, and one question.

Kids at the edge of a pond. A stick, a jar, a dare. Somebody pokes at a frog to see it jump. Nobody's being evil; they're curious, and bored, and in a group. The Udana has a scene like that. The Buddha is walking between the city of Savatthi and the monastery at Jeta's Grove, and on the way he sees a crowd of boys tormenting fish. He could walk past. He could scold. He does neither. He stops, and asks them a question.
screen: `A STICK, A JAR, A DARE.` → `ON THE ROAD TO JETA'S GROVE.` → `HE STOPS AND ASKS.`

segments.voice: Boys, he says, are you afraid of pain? Do you dislike pain? Yes, sir, they say. We're afraid of pain. We don't like it. Two questions, two honest answers. Then, knowing the meaning of it, he speaks the verse. If you fear pain, if you dislike pain, don't do a bad deed, openly or in secret. If you do, or are doing one, you won't be free of pain, even if you run and fly away. Notice the method. He doesn't begin with the fish. He begins with the boys. He doesn't tell them what fish feel; he asks what they feel. Once they've said it out loud, the rest follows on its own: if you don't like pain, you already know something about everyone who can feel it. The Dhammapada has the same insight in its chapter on punishment: everyone trembles at the rod; putting yourself in their place, don't strike or cause to strike. The Udana gives it a scene and a pond. And the verse doesn't threaten the boys with a stranger's punishment. It points at the plain logic of cause and result: what you do follows you, even if you run. It's the thread of only by deeds and fear from the rod, a few days back, now with a pond.
screen: `ARE YOU AFRAID OF PAIN?` · `START WITH THE BOYS, NOT THE FISH.` · `OPENLY OR IN SECRET.` · `EVEN IF YOU RUN.` · then, large: `ALL DISLIKE PAIN.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself the Buddha's question honestly, do I dislike pain, and feel the answer in the body. Let your mind go outward, to a coworker, a stranger on the bus, a dog in the street, a fish in a pond, each of whom would answer the same. Then look for one small cruelty in your own day, a cutting joke, an impatient shove, a creature swatted without thinking, and simply see it.
Dukkha, pain. In the Udana, the Buddha asks boys tormenting fish whether they dislike dukkha, and lets their answer teach them.
Your line: all dislike pain. The boys knew it the moment they said it out loud. That's day six hundred fifteen.

616.title: Dearer than oneself
616.hook: King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika agree no one is dearer than oneself; so harm no other
616.howItsDone: Teachers of metta, loving-kindness, often begin with goodwill toward oneself and then extend the same wish to others, and some cite the verse to Pasenadi and Mallika as the reason.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dukkha, and the boys at the pond who said they fear pain. Your line: all dislike pain. Today closes a week, with a king and a queen on a palace roof.

A palace roof, a husband and a wife, and a question that's half tender and half a test. King Pasenadi of Kosala, whom you've met kissing the Buddha's feet, is on the upper terrace of his palace with Queen Mallika. And he asks her: Mallika, is there anyone dearer to you than yourself? It's not hard to imagine what answer a husband might hope for. The text doesn't say what he hoped. It says what she said.
screen: `A PALACE ROOF.` → `A TENDER QUESTION, AND A TEST.` → `IS ANYONE DEARER THAN YOURSELF?`

segments.voice: No, your majesty, Mallika says. There is no one dearer to me than myself. And is there anyone dearer to you than yourself? The king thinks, and says: no, Mallika, for me too, there is no one dearer than myself. It's a startlingly honest exchange between a husband and a wife. Pasenadi goes down from the palace and tells the Buddha. And the Buddha, knowing the meaning of this, speaks the verse. Searching all directions with the mind, one finds no one anywhere dearer than oneself. In the same way, each person holds themselves dear. So one who loves himself should not harm another. Look at what just happened. Something that sounds selfish, I love myself most, turns in two lines into the ground of kindness. The verse takes their honesty and turns it outward: if it's true for me, it's true for everyone. The week behind: Upasiva's crossing, the Udana opening, doubts vanishing under the tree, Bahiya in the street and no time to lose, the boys at the pond, and now the palace roof. Yesterday the logic of pain, today the logic of love: the same step from me to you.
screen: `NO ONE DEARER THAN MYSELF.` · `THE KING SAYS THE SAME.` · `EACH HOLDS THEMSELVES DEAR.` · `SO HARM NO OTHER.` · then, large: `EVERYONE LOVES THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: Notice, without judgment, how much you want to be safe, to be well, to be treated fairly, and let that be fully true. Then bring to mind someone you'll see today, maybe someone difficult, sitting somewhere with exactly the same wish, just as strong. Hold both at once for a few breaths.
Piya, dear or beloved. King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika agree no one is dearer to them than themselves, and the Buddha turns it into a reason not to harm.
Your line: everyone loves themselves. That's where kindness can quietly start. A full week, done.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. a king tells you that he and his queen each love themselves more than anyone. what do you say?
options: that's selfish; love others more.
since everyone holds themselves this dear, harm no one.
that's a private matter.
fork.reveal: he doesn't argue with them. he takes what they've found and turns it outward: as you are dear to yourself, so others are to themselves.

original.note: Pali piya: dear, beloved. the question is whether anyone is piyatara, dearer, than oneself.

trapdoor: what you thought: loving yourself most is selfish.
what it means: in Udana 5.1 it's the starting point: because everyone holds themselves dear, no one should harm another.
what a scholar hears: the same conversation and verse appear in the Samyutta Nikaya (SN 3.8, Mallika Sutta).

chat.says: Wasn't it selfish of Mallika to say no one was dearer to her than herself?
options: The Buddha turned it outward: all hold themselves dear, so harm no one.
Yes; the Buddha scolded her and told her to love the king more.
No; the verse says care for yourself and let others fend for themselves.
chat.meaning: The verse turns their honesty outward: each person holds themselves dear, so one who loves himself should not harm another.
